chunks: From him, from Yaqub ibn Yazeed, from Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Yazeed, from his father, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I eat good food, smell pleasant scents, ride luxurious animals, and a servant follows me. If you see any arrogance in this, I will not do it.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) paused, then said, 'The accursed tyrant is the one who belittles people and ignores the truth.' Umar said, 'As for the truth, I do not ignore it, but I do not know what belittling is.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'The one who considers people insignificant and is arrogant over them, that is the tyrant.'

key_terms.أَطْرَقَ: He paused or remained silent for a moment
key_terms.التَّجَبُّر: Arrogance, haughtiness, or acting superior over others
key_terms.الْجَبَّار: The tyrant or the arrogant one who dominates others
key_terms.الْغَمْص: Belittling, slighting, or looking down on people
key_terms.الْفَارِهَة: Luxurious or fine animal (used for riding)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between enjoying worldly comforts and true arrogance (tajabbur) in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between permissible worldly pleasures (*al-tajabbur* in a superficial sense) and true spiritual arrogance (*al-jabbar*), which is rooted in social contempt and intellectual rigidity. This clarification aligns with Shia ethical teachings that prioritize inner humility over external asceticism, warning against the 'cursed arrogance' that leads to distancing oneself from the truth. The Imam’s definition emphasizes that arrogance is a relational and cognitive failure—looking down on others and rejecting truth—rather than merely a lack of material simplicity.
